title: Benchmark FieldVec dot product against fflas-ffpack fdot for GF(p)
description:
Install fflas-ffpack and benchmark our delayed-reduction `FieldVec::dot_product` for Fp

against fflas-ffpack's `fdot` for equivalent prime field sizes. ## Setup - fflas-ffpack and givaro are installed system-wide - C++ benchmark harness: `benches/fflas_fdot_bench.cpp` - Build script: `benches/build_fflas_bench.sh` - Rust benchmarks: `crates/gf2-core/benches/fieldvec_dot_product.rs` ## Measured results (n=1000) | Prime | gf2-core (ns/elem) | fflas int64 (ns/elem) | fflas double (ns/elem) | Ratio vs int64 | |-------|--------------------|-----------------------|------------------------|----------------| | p=65521 | 1.72 | 0.49 | 0.11 (BLAS) | 3.5× | | p=2^31-1 | 1.77 | 1.11 | n/a | 1.6× | | p~2^62 | 2.72 | **not supported** | n/a | gf2-core only | ## Analysis - **Medium primes (p ~ 2^31)**: Within 2× of fflas-ffpack (1.6× ratio). Our Montgomery + delayed reduction is competitive. - **Small primes (p < 2^16)**: 3.5× slower than fflas-ffpack's `Modular` path. fflas-ffpack uses simpler modular arithmetic (no Montgomery) and benefits from compiler autovectorization. The `Modular` BLAS path (~0.11 ns/elem) uses hardware SIMD FMA, which we can't match without floating-point conversion. - **Large primes (p ~ 2^62)**: fflas-ffpack cannot handle primes this large (Modular max cardinality ~2^31). gf2-core is the only option in this regime. ## Success criteria - Dot product throughput within 2× of fflas-ffpack's `fdot` for medium primes (p ~ 2^31): **met** (1.6×) - Large primes (p ~ 2^62): fflas-ffpack unsupported, gf2-core uniquely serves this regime - Small primes (p < 2^16): 3.5× gap due to fflas-ffpack's simpler modular arithmetic and BLAS paths. Closing this gap requires floating-point conversion or specialized small-prime kernels (future optimization) - Benchmark results documented as committed evidence in benchmark file doc comments - C++ fflas-ffpack harness is reproducible via `benches/build_fflas_bench.sh`
